prompt:

   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: ADP is a top dog in its industry with a well-known brand, but payroll is a mature industry rather than an emerging one, and revenue grows about 7% a year. It lacks the fast-growth, visionary-founder and 'overvalued' traits Gardner prizes, so it fits Rule Breaker investing poorly.
summaries.buffett: ADP fits many Buffett tenets: a simple, essential business with sticky customers (92.1% retention), high returns on capital, steady growth, 51 straight years of dividend increases and consistent buybacks. The main gap is price: at about 26 times trailing earnings there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the durable, easy-to-understand toll-road economics, the float from about $40B of client funds and the rational capital allocation. Inverting, the main ways to fail are AI-native rivals and a shrinking workforce, which look slow-moving, but the price is full rather than wonderful.
summaries.lynch: ADP is a classic stalwart: a large, reliable grower with EPS up about 9-11% a year and a familiar story. Its P/E of roughly 26 is well above its growth rate, so Lynch's PEG test fails, and it is far from overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: ADP keeps developing new products (Lyric HCM, ADP Assist, HCM agents, Workforce Suite), has a famously strong sales force and expanding margins, and management is candid. Growth is moderate rather than outstanding, so it is a solid but not exceptional Fisher holding.
summaries.graham: ADP passes Graham's tests for size, a long dividend record and ten-year earnings growth (EPS $3.25 in FY2016 to $10.94 in FY2026). It fails the valuation tests badly: about 26 times earnings and a P/E times P/B near 490 versus Graham's limit of 22.5.
summaries.thiel: ADP is a strong incumbent with a powerful sales channel and durable position, but it does not own a technology ten times better than rivals and is not pursuing a secret that others miss. It is a good business in a competitive market rather than a Thiel-style monopoly built from zero to one.
summaries.gerstner: ADP shows the operating discipline Gerstner praises: flat headcount, AI-driven productivity and 70-90 bps of margin expansion guided for FY2027 alongside large buybacks. But growth of 5-6% and a premium multiple make it an efficiency story rather than the high-growth compounder he usually targets.
summaries.druckenmiller: The stock has rebounded about 35% since late April 2026 after the AI-disruption selloff, and earnings beat in each of the last eight quarters, but estimates are rising only modestly. Falling interest rates would reduce client-fund income, so the macro backdrop is not clearly in its favour.
summaries.smith: ADP fits Terry Smith's 'good company' test well: high returns on capital (ROIC about 60%), cash conversion above 100% of net income, resilient recurring revenue and modest capital needs. The question is 'don't overpay': a free-cash-flow yield of about 4.6% is reasonable rather than cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: ADP scores very well on return on capital but only moderately on earnings yield, with operating profit about 5% of enterprise value. It would rank as a quality business at a middling price in the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: ADP has two legs of Akre's stool: an extraordinary business with high returns and switching costs, and capable, owner-friendly management. The third leg, reinvesting at high rates, is weaker because most cash goes to dividends and buybacks rather than growth.
summaries.pabrai: ADP is a low-risk business with a small chance of permanent loss, but it is neither distressed nor cheap. The early-2026 selloff to about $188 was the kind of temporary setback Pabrai seeks, yet at $286 most of that discount has gone.
summaries.wood: ADP is not a disruptive-innovation company: it is an incumbent adopting AI rather than leading one of ARK's platforms. It fits Cathie Wood's approach poorly and could be on the losing side of AI-driven disruption of HR software.
summaries.ackman: ADP resembles Ackman's ideal of a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generating business with high barriers to entry and modest debt. Interest-rate sensitivity of client-fund income and the premium valuation are the main reservations.
summaries.sleep: ADP uses its scale mainly to widen margins rather than to pass savings back to customers in Nomad's 'scale economies shared' sense. It is a durable franchise, but not one clearly getting stronger relative to rivals over 10-20 years.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, fast-growing new markets and technical founders, which ADP, founded in 1949, does not offer. It solves a painful problem for employers, but it is a mature incumbent rather than a venture-style opportunity.
summaries.nash: ADP is a high-quality, mature compounder but fails several of Nash's instant-kill and valuation screens: revenue growth below 10% and slowing (6.7%), more debt than corporate cash, and a price above his DCF value even at a 10% discount rate. It scores about 70 on his 13 categories, below the 75 threshold.

momentum.evidence: ADP rose about 35% from roughly $212 at end-April 2026 to $285.84 on Oct 19, 2026, beating the S&P 500, but it is up only about 1.8% over 52 weeks.

g4.evidence: Management under CEO Maria Black executes well, and director Robert Swan bought about $746k of stock in May 2026, but ADP is not backed by famous lead investors; about 91% of shares are held by institutions.

g6.evidence: Commentators flagged the premium P/E, and the consensus rating is Hold with an average target ($286.40) at the current price, but few call it wildly overvalued.

simple.evidence: ADP runs payroll, HR software and co-employment for employers and earns fees plus interest on client funds, which a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2021 to FY2026 ($15.0B to $21.9B), and ADP has raised its dividend for 51 consecutive years.

integrity.evidence: ADP gives clear annual guidance, has beaten EPS consensus in each of the last eight quarters, returns cash through dividends and buybacks, and has no governance controversies.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions are small and focused (FY2026 spending $22.8M; Workforce Software in FY2025 for about $1.17B), and management says deals must fit strategically, culturally and financially.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 60% (StockAnalysis), with debt of $5.1B against $5.8B of operating income, so returns do not rely on leverage.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $5,244.6M (operating cash flow $5,441.2M less $196.6M capex), about 119% of net earnings of $4,413.5M.

b10.evidence: Over FY2021-FY2026 diluted EPS rose from $6.07 to $10.94 while most earnings were paid out, showing retained capital earned very high returns.

safety.evidence: At $285.84 the stock trades above a Nash-style DCF value of about $240 per share even at a 10% discount rate, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 23 times FY2027 consensus EPS of $12.26 and a 4.6% free-cash-flow yield is fair for a high-quality, 5-6% revenue grower but not a bargain.

mu5.evidence: Failure would require clients to abandon a mission-critical system with 92.1% retention; the realistic risks (AI rivals, lower employment, lower rates) erode growth rather than threaten survival.

reinvest.evidence: ADP reinvests at high returns in R&D ($1,028.8M in FY2026) and products, but the business needs little capital, so most cash ($4.7B in FY2026) goes to dividends and buybacks.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart: steady 6-7% revenue growth, about 10% EPS growth and a simple story of more clients, more products and margin expansion.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 26 is far above the expected EPS growth of 9%-11% guided for FY2027.

runway.evidence: International payroll, Lyric HCM, workforce management and AI agents offer room to grow, but consensus sees only about 5-6% annual revenue growth.

ly7.evidence: The company cut diluted shares from 428.1M (FY2021) to 403.3M (FY2026), but insiders are mostly sellers, including CEO Maria Black selling about $8.4M in September 2026.

ly8.evidence: ADP is a $113B company covered by many analysts and its jobs report is widely followed, so it is not overlooked.

fi2.evidence: ADP launched Lyric HCM (live clients up 94% in Q4 FY2026), ADP Assist and HCM agents for nearly all 1.1M clients as older platforms mature.

fi3.evidence: R&D of about $1.03B a year produces steady new products and rising margins, but has not yet made ADP the clear product leader against Workday or Rippling.

fi4.evidence: ADP's large direct sales force produced $2.2B of Employer Services new business bookings in FY2026, up 6%.

longterm.evidence: Management invests steadily in new platforms and AI, but also targets annual margin expansion and EPS growth, balancing long-term and short-term goals.

gr1.evidence: ADP had $21.9B of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $113B.

ni10.evidence: ADP has been profitable throughout the last decade, with net earnings rising from $1,492.5M in FY2016 to $4,413.5M in FY2026.

gr4.evidence: ADP raised its dividend for the 51st consecutive year in November 2025, to $1.70 a quarter.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $3.25 in FY2016 to $10.94 in FY2026, an increase of about 237%.

gr6.evidence: The stock trades at about 26 times FY2026 diluted EPS of $10.94, well above 15 times.

gr7.evidence: With a P/E near 26 and price-to-book near 19 (equity $6.03B), P/E x P/B is about 490, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: ADP's software is competitive, but no one considers it ten times better than Workday, Paychex or Rippling.

timing.evidence: Demand for outsourced HR and compliance is steady, but AI is both an opportunity (agents) and a threat (AI-native rivals, leaner workforces) right now.

th3.evidence: ADP began in 1949 helping local business owners pay their workers and expanded to more than 1.1 million clients in 140+ countries, but that monopoly-style expansion is decades behind it.

team.evidence: Maria Black and CFO Peter Hadley run the company competently, with eight straight EPS beats, but they are capable stewards rather than a world-famous team.

th5.evidence: ADP's distribution is a key strength: a large direct sales force and partner channels that produced $2.2B of FY2026 new bookings.

durable.evidence: Switching costs and compliance know-how should keep ADP important for decades, but AI-native platforms and leaner workforces could erode its share and pricing.

th7.evidence: Payroll outsourcing is a well-understood market with many competitors; ADP has no unique hidden opportunity.

trend.evidence: ADP is adding AI agents and benefits from the HR-outsourcing trend, but it is not a leading beneficiary of AI and is seen by investors as potentially threatened by it.

dr1.evidence: FY2027 guidance calls for adjusted EPS growth of 9%-11%, similar to FY2026's 11%, so earnings are steady rather than accelerating.

dr2.evidence: Margin expansion of 70-90 bps and buybacks should lift results by FY2028, but this is largely expected by the market.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would cut client-fund interest income ($1,354.8M in FY2026), and slower hiring weighs on pays per control (+1% in FY2026).

dr6.evidence: Q1 FY2027 results on Oct 28, 2026, Lyric HCM adoption and AI-agent monetisation are possible catalysts, but none is transformative.

dr7.evidence: Growth of 5-6% and a full valuation do not justify a large concentrated position for a growth-oriented macro investor.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 46.4% in FY2026, diluted by PEO revenue, rising from 42.4% in FY2021, but below pure software peers like Paychex (about 74%).

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $5,244.6M is about 4.6% of a $113.7B market value, reasonable for a business of this quality and stability.

gb2.evidence: Operating income of $5,779.0M is about 5.0% of an enterprise value of about $114.6B, a moderate earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The early-2026 drop to about $188 on AI-disruption and jobs fears looked like a temporary setback, but the stock has since recovered to about $286.

pa4.evidence: With 92.1% retention, $5.4B of operating cash flow and modest corporate debt, the risk of permanent capital loss is low.

wo1.evidence: ADP uses AI in its products but is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its costs fall gradually with scale (margin up about 4 points in five years), not the steep cost declines that open up huge new demand.

wo3.evidence: It combines cloud software and AI assistants, but not several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market is employers' HR and payroll spending, which grows steadily but will not multiply in five years.

ac3.evidence: ADP has no commodity exposure, but its revenue depends on employment levels and $1,354.8M of FY2026 revenue came from interest on client funds, which is rate-sensitive.

ns1.evidence: ADP keeps scale gains as margin expansion (operating margin 22.2% to 26.3% over FY2021-FY2026) rather than cutting prices for customers.

ns4.evidence: ADP should remain a leader, but whether it will be clearly stronger in 10-20 years is uncertain given AI-native competition.

va2.evidence: Paying staff correctly and complying with tax rules in many jurisdictions is a large, painful problem for over a million employers.

tn1.evidence: ADP is a 1949-founded incumbent retrofitting AI into payroll, not a company built for a major secular trend.

tn2.evidence: The market feared ADP was an AI loser in early 2026, while it reports AI agents reaching nearly all 1.1M clients and flat headcount; but this gap has largely closed with the rebound.

tn3.evidence: ADP is a large-cap U.S. company and not a commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year and the company is very profitable (FY2026 net margin 20.1%), though debt ($5.1B) slightly exceeds corporate cash ($4.23B), with interest well covered.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow is consistently positive, but debt exceeded corporate cash at both June 30, 2025 ($8.8B vs $7.8B incl. securities) and June 30, 2026 ($5.1B vs $4.2B).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 6.7% in FY2026 and is guided to 5%-6% for FY2027.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 6.7% plus an FCF margin of 23.9% gives about 31, below 40.

tn8.evidence: FY2026 revenue rose 6.74% while total expenses rose 6.55% ($15,604.9M to $16,627.7M).

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: debt ($5.1B) exceeds corporate cash ($4.2B), and revenue growth is below 10% and slowing (7.1% in FY2025 to 6.7% in FY2026).

tn10.evidence: No major regulatory or legal threat is disclosed; payroll and PEO regulation is a normal operating cost.

tn11.evidence: ADP provides payroll, HR and co-employment services that help employers pay staff correctly and stay compliant, charging per-employee subscription fees plus PEO fees and earning interest on client funds.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10 (26.3%), short interest 10 (2.8%), institutional ownership 10 (91%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and operating margin rose from 22.2% to 26.3%, but free cash flow dipped in FY2024 ($3,949.2M vs $4,001.3M) and debt exceeded corporate cash in FY2025 and FY2026.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 12.6x and the current ratio about 1.05, but because client fund obligations ($44.4B) sit on the balance sheet, liabilities are about 9.5x equity and assets ex-goodwill only about 1.05x liabilities.

tn18.evidence: Maria Black has executed well since 2023, but she is not a founder, has under 10 years as CEO and sold about $8.4M of stock in September 2026 rather than buying.

tn20.evidence: ADP beat consensus adjusted EPS in each of the last eight quarters, including $2.64 vs $2.60 in Q4 FY2026.

tn21.evidence: There is no fraud, auditor change (Deloitte) or acquisition spree and margins are rising, but insiders including the CEO sold after the stock's rebound in September 2026.

tn22.evidence: ADP has $21.9B of revenue, strong profits and shrinking share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At $285.84 the price implies about 11% annual revenue growth with a 22.6% FCF margin at a 10% discount rate, above the 6.8% three-year average ADP is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using 6.8% growth and a 22.6% FCF margin (3-year averages), 4% terminal growth and net debt of $0.9B, value is about $179 per share at 12% (about $240 at 10%), below $285.84.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 23 on FY2027 consensus EPS of $12.26 against 9%-11% EPS growth gives a PEG of about 2.3, well above 1.
